short: Four centuries of Chinese rule that set the template for imperial government.
full:
Liu Bang, a village official turned rebel, defeated Xiang Yu and was proclaimed emperor in 202 BCE; the alternative date of 206 BCE marks only his appointment as King of Han. The dynasty kept the centralised bureaucracy the Qin had built but dropped its harshest legalism, recruiting officials by recommendation and, increasingly, by Confucian learning. Emperor Wu drove the frontier into Central Asia against the Xiongnu, opening the routes later called the Silk Road, and imposed state monopolies on salt and iron.

Wang Mang's Xin interregnum from 9 to 23 CE splits the dynasty into Western and Eastern Han, the restored court ruling from Luoyang. Paper, the seismoscope and a census counting nearly sixty million people belong to this period. Eunuch factions at court, the Yellow Turban rebellion of 184 and the warlord generals who suppressed it hollowed the state out, and in 220 CE Emperor Xian abdicated to Cao Pi. Chinese still call themselves the Han.
